newsitem.title: USA: Sharon urges continued U.S. investment in Israel.
newsitem.headline: Sharon urges continued U.S. investment in Israel.

text.p: Israeli Minister of National Infrastructures Ariel Sharon on Tuesday downplayed tensions in the Middle East and urged U.S. investors not to be deterred by recent violence in Israel.
Sharon said that the conflict between Arabs and Jews has been going on for a century and that the road to peace was a long and painful one.
He spoke at the start of the Israel-North America Business Conference in New York, held for investors interested in bidding on $50 billion of Israeli infrastructural projects.

"I don't think there should be anything that would frighten (investors)," he said in an interview. "There may be some questions, but only for short periods....I don't think that should interfere with the wish to invest in Israel."
He declined to comment specifically on political developments other than to say that he was convinced peace would be achieved and that foreign investors had little to worry about in the long run.

Sharon told a news conference that his country planned to invest $5.5 billion in developing water sources, desalination projects and recycling of sewage water. Israel would invest $6.0 billion in roads and $3.0 billion in railroads, he added.

He also said that up to one million Jews could migrate to Israel from the former Soviet Union, facilitating the need for apartments to be built at a rate of 80,000 annually during the next five years.

Israel last week was rocked by violence in which 59 Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers were killed. The unrest led to a hastily convened summit in Washington between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
"Peace is something hard. It's painful. Sometimes it's painful like war," Sharon told a news conference. "One must make concessions. It is hard but it will happen."

"The question being discussed in Israel is ... how to provide, together with peace, the needed security," he said. "Sometimes it is better to have difficulties now and have questions that should be asked now rather than later when friction and tension could bring war."
